title: Daughters and sons
hookLine: He gives daughters to whom He wills, sons, or both, or none (42:49–50)

lines: A FACE DARKENS AT A DAUGHTER.
FOR WHAT SIN WAS SHE KILLED?
cards: A man is told his wife has given birth to a girl. His face darkens. He hides from people, ashamed of the news, wondering whether to keep her or bury her in the dust.

The Qur'an describes this scene from the Arabia it came down into, and it clearly wants the scene to end. Surah An-Nahl paints it; Surah At-Takwir says the buried girl will one day be asked for what sin she was killed.
Against that background, listen to the order of the words in Surah Ash-Shura when it talks about children: who gets named first.

teach.b: Verse forty-nine. To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Pickthall: "He createth what He will."

Then: He gives daughters to whomever He wills, and sons to whomever He wills. Daughters first. In a culture where a daughter's birth could darken a father's face, the Qur'an lists girls ahead of boys, as gifts.
Some early scholars noticed this; one is reported to have said it's a blessing for a woman when her first child is a girl, because Allah began with daughters.
Verse fifty continues: or He gives both, sons and daughters, and He makes whom He wills childless. He is Knowing, Able.
Four possibilities: daughters, sons, both, or none, every one placed in Allah's hands.

teach.h: NOT A VERDICT ON THE PARENTS.
teach.b: Teachers draw from this that none of them is a verdict on the parents. Not a reward for having sons. Not a punishment for having daughters, or no children at all.

The Qur'an's stories and the Prophet's life bear it out. Ibrahim and Zakariyya were old when sons were given. 'A'isha, wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, had no children, and companions came to her with their questions.
The Prophet himself had sons who died young, and it was through his daughter Fatima that his family continued.

And a hadith in Sahih Muslim gives raising girls a special honor: whoever raises two daughters until they're grown, the Prophet said, will come on the Day of Resurrection with me like this, and he held two fingers together.
The verse lists four gifts, and the hadith makes sure the first is never treated as the lesser.

how: Muslims greet the birth of a child with thanks to Allah and often an 'aqiqah celebration for both girls and boys; the hadith on raising daughters is widely taught as an honor for parents of girls.

o: an inheritance passed down to the eldest
a gift, freely given, as children are
a reward earned for faithful service

games.q: daughters and sons — tap the pairs.
p: no children, a teacher many came to
with the Prophet, like two fingers

s: the verse names sons before daughters
daughters come first: He gives daughters to whom He wills, and sons to whom He wills.
the verse treats childlessness as a punishment
it places all four, including none, in Allah's knowing hands.
the Prophet's family continued through his daughter Fatima
his sons died young; his descendants come through Fatima.

games.q: in a culture where some men grieved at a daughter's birth, the Qur'an lists the gifts of children. which does it name first?
games.why: daughters, then sons, then both, then none: every one of them Allah's to give.

practice: Bring to mind the children around you, one by one: your own, if you have them, nieces and nephews, students, a friend's baby, the child you once were, and picture each face for a breath.
If you pray, thank Allah for each one; if not, simply be grateful. And if there's an ache here, a child hoped for or lost, let it be part of the sitting too.

wordCard.voice: Hiba, gift, the sense behind Ash-Shura's yahab, Allah's giving of daughters, sons, both, or none, with daughters named first. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: He gives daughters to whom He wills; yahab is the verb of giving a gift (hiba).

carryVoice: Your line: each gift is his. Daughters, sons, both, or none, and none of it a verdict. That's day five hundred sixty-nine.
